newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Unions threaten blockade of BHP exports.
newsitem.headline: Unions threaten blockade of BHP exports.

text.p: As Australia's steelmaker the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) prepares to retreat from competition in heavy steel products on Asian markets, trade unions are preparing to block its exports of raw materials to Asian steel producers.

The Australian Workers Union (AWU), the body most affected by BHP's decision to phase out its Newcastle steelworks, will hold a meeting with the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) on Monday to request support from other unions, Maurie Rudd, AWU Newcastle secretary, said on Wednesday.
This would follow a mass meeting of AWU Newcastle members on Friday.
Rudd said a threatened blockade of all of BHP's exports would be designed to bring BHP back to the negotiating table on closure of the Newcastle works.
But AWU national vice-president Vern Faulconer said it was too early to pre-empt decisions by Friday's meeting by commenting on a possible national union blockade of BHP exports.

BHP is Australia's largest exporter of coal and iron ore. BHP's decision to close the Newcastle works, which has a capacity of two million tonnes of steel a year, signals an exit by the Australian group as a medium-level player on Asian heavy steel product export markets.
BHP has conceded a clear victory to Asian steelmakers by deciding to withdraw from the export of almost one million tonnes of steel products, statements by the company show.
"The bottom line is that we're exiting about 800,000-900,000 tonnes of export," John Devers, BHP Steel's public affairs chief, told Reuters on Wednesday.

The export products which BHP will chop from 1999 when the Newcastle blast furnaces will be closed will be mainly slabs, blooms, structural and universal beams, currently produced at the group's Whyalla plant in South Australia, he said.
Whyalla will shift to producing billets for feed while Newcastle will stop producing billets.
BHP will shift to higher value-added flat products from heavier semi-finished lower-value products, Devers said.
BHP's overall steel production is expected to decline by a net 300,000-400,000 tonnes from the end of 1999 when the front end of Newcastle was closed, Devers said.

This would occur as a net result of the loss of 800,000-900,000 tonnes of production now exported but an increase in production by the Port Kembla plant, near Wollongong, by 500,000 tonnes to 5.0 million tonnes, he said.

The re-organisation would mean that BHP steel rolling and coating plants in Asia would source from anywhere, including from producers such as South Korea's Pohang Iron and Steel Co Ltd (POSCO), he said.
POSCO is cited by BHP as having set international productivity standards of 1,000 tonnes of steel per employee a year. BHP's productivity is presently about 700 tonnes of steel per employee a year.
It was not known if the reorganisation would also cause a jump in imports of steel product into Australia by BHP, he said.
BHP steel exports in the year to May 31 1996 rose by two percent to 3.393 million tonnes from total production of 8.624 million tonnes, up two percent.
